desc:
In one operation you may add 1 to, or subtract 1 from, any single element of nums. The median is the element at zero-based position n // 2 after sorting (the larger middle value when n is even).

Return the minimum number of operations after which the median of the array equals target.

nums = [2, 5, 6, 8, 5], target = 4
sorted [2, 5, 5, 6, 8]; change one 5 to 4 (the median) and the other 5 to 4
-> [2, 4, 4, 6, 8], median 4, 2 operations
answer = 2
hints: After the changes, the element in the median position equals target, everything to its left is at most target and everything to its right is at least target.
Sort first. Which elements of the sorted array can stay exactly where they are without cost?
In sorted order: lower-half elements larger than target must come down, upper-half elements smaller than target must come up, and the median element itself must move to target. Sum these distances.
editorial: Sort a and let mid = n // 2. Moving an element only changes the sorted order if it crosses another one, and the cheapest way to produce a median of exactly target is to keep the sorted order: the first mid elements must end up at most target, the element at mid must be exactly target, and the remaining ones at least target.
Therefore the cost is |a[mid] - target| plus max(0, a[i] - target) for every i < mid plus max(0, target - a[i]) for every i > mid. Elements already on the correct side cost nothing.
Sorting dominates: O(n log n). The answer is at most 6,000 * 2 * 10<sup>5</sup>, which fits easily in 32 bits.
